_note: INDUSTRIAL CHEMICALS. Every number here is stoichiometry (molar masses, reaction equations), a documented ore/feedstock assay, or a fuel-energy estimate built the same way lime_kg's entry builds one (theoretical heat of reaction/vaporisation, divided by a stated kiln/furnace efficiency, divided by a fuel calorific value) - never a figure backed out of data/prices.json. Several genuinely different industries that make the SAME output are kept as separate entries under different keys, exactly like brass_kg/brass_direct_alloy_kg in 20_nonferrous.json: sulfuric_acid_kg (lead chamber) vs sulfuric_acid_vitriol_kg (dry-distilled oil of vitriol); salt_kg (rock salt) vs salt_solar_kg (solar pans) vs salt_brine_kg (brine boiling); sodium_carbonate_kg (Leblanc) vs sodium_carbonate_solvay_kg (Solvay). pyrolusite_kg is a material this family needs (bleach_kg's chlorine stage) but is NOT redefined here - it already has an entry in 20_nonferrous.json. Four intermediates this family needs but the tree does not yet carry - sodium_carbonate_kg (soda ash), citric_acid_kg, camphor_kg, and the Solvay alternate - are defined here the same way 20_nonferrous.json added calamine_kg and galena_kg: new keys, each with its own physically-argued entry, per _SCHEMA.md's 'new ones you also define an entry for'. nitric_acid_kg, nitre_kg, nitroglycerin_kg and nitrocellulose_kg are OUT OF SCOPE for this file by instruction: where a recipe genuinely needs one (hydrogen peroxide bleaching stages do not, but celluloid_kg genuinely needs nitrocellulose_kg), it is referenced as an existing tree material key with a note that its own production entry is a deliberate, recorded gap - never described.

sulfur_kg.extracted_from: ore deposit (native volcanic sulphur beds, e.g. Sicily)
sulfur_kg.basis: per tonne of refined, kiln-melted elemental sulphur
sulfur_kg.yield_basis: EXTRACTED, but the refining step destroys much of what is mined, which belongs in this entry rather than a separate one because Sicilian sulphur ore was never sold or moved unrefined - it was refined at the pit mouth. Sicilian sulphur-bearing rock (gypsum/limestone matrix with embedded native sulphur crystals) assays roughly 25-30% elemental sulphur by mass, taken here at 27%. The historical 'calcarone' kiln melts this out by burning part of the sulphur itself as fuel - sulphur ignites around 250 C and melts at only 115 C, so a stack of ore can be lit and the melt run off without any external fuel at all - but that self-firing is exactly why the process is so wasteful: roughly a third to two-fifths of the CONTAINED sulphur is consumed as its own heat source rather than recovered, a well-documented historical inefficiency and the reason later Gill kilns and eventually the Frasch hot-water process (1894) replaced it. Taking 60% overall recovery of contained sulphur (27% ore assay x 60% kiln recovery), one tonne of refined sulphur needs about 6.2 t of ore. Labour is mining the soft, friable sedimentary ore plus stacking and breaking open the kiln - no furnaceman is listed because the kiln needs no tending fuel, only loading and clearing.

capital.good: lead chamber (sheet lead lining and timber framing)
capital.capital_basis: The lead chamber process this entry's own yield_basis describes is named for its capital good: a large chamber lined in sheet lead, chosen specifically because lead resists sulphuric acid attack better than other cheap metals of the era, run inside a timber frame housing. This is close to a pure case of capital expressed as a material the system already prices - the chamber is, physically, mostly lead, priced by this file's own lead_kg entry, and 'plumber' (from plumbum, lead) is the historically exact trade name for the workers who made and maintained sheet-lead chambers, which the wage table already carries. Lead's acid resistance is real but not infinite, and chambers are documented as needing periodic re-sheeting rather than lasting indefinitely; 15 years reflects that lead is the most durable of this file's capital linings even though it is also the most expensive by mass. Annual output reflects a substantial 19th-century works rather than a small workshop-scale operation.

sulfuric_acid_kg.basis: per tonne of lead-chamber sulphuric acid at commercial chamber strength, ~65% H2SO4 by mass
sulfuric_acid_kg.yield_basis: THE INDUSTRIAL ROUTE (Roebuck, 1746 onward), stoichiometric net reaction S + 3/2 O2 + H2O -> H2SO4. H2SO4 is 98.08 g/mol, sulphur 32.07 g/mol, so pure sulphur needed is 32.7% of the pure-acid mass produced; at 65% acid strength a tonne of output contains 650 kg pure H2SO4, needing 212.6 kg sulphur stoichiometrically. Real chamber conversion runs on the order of 85% efficient (gas leakage past the lead seams, incomplete nitrous-gas catalysis), giving the 250 kg figure. Nitre (saltpetre) is not consumed by the acid-forming reaction itself - it supplies the NO/NO2 that catalyses SO2+O2+H2O -> H2SO4 - but real chambers lose nitrogen oxides out the stack faster than the sulphur dioxide, so continuous make-up nitre on the order of 7-10% of the sulphur burned (taken at 8%) was a standard historical consumption figure, not a stoichiometric one. Water covers the ~120 kg chemically combined in the H2SO4 itself (18.02/98.08 g water per g acid, scaled to 650 kg acid), the roughly 350 kg of plain dilution water that brings the theoretical ~78% chamber-strength acid down to the commercial 65% grade, and a further margin for the continuous water spray real Gay-Lussac/Glover towers ran (most recirculated, but not all - some genuinely leaves as vapour carried out with the vented gas stream) - a generous single-pass figure rather than a figure that assumes a recycling loop this entry cannot verify. Note also that the reaction gains mass from atmospheric oxygen (S + O2 -> SO2 -> SO3, absorbing roughly 1.5 kg of O2 per kg of sulphur burned) exactly the way rust or any oxidation does; that oxygen is free, untracked air, which is why the tracked inputs by mass do not have to sum to the full output mass on their own. Sulphur combustion is exothermic and the chambers are close to self-heating; the small charcoal figure is only for cold-weather start-up and auxiliary steam, not the main reaction. nitre_kg has no production entry in this file - out of scope by instruction - so this entry treats it as a purchased input, which is exactly how a chamber-acid works fed on saltpetre bought from a nitre bed.

sulfuric_acid_vitriol_kg.basis: per tonne of concentrated 'oil of vitriol' (~95% H2SO4), the strong acid obtained by dry-distilling calcined green vitriol
sulfuric_acid_vitriol_kg.yield_basis: THE EARLIER ROUTE, genuinely a different industry from the chamber process rather than a smaller version of it: alchemists and early chemists (attested from the medieval Islamic world through Libavius and Glauber in the 16-17th century) drove concentrated fuming acid out of green vitriol (ferrous sulphate, FeSO4.7H2O, already priced in this dataset as green_vitriol_kg, gathered by weathering pyrite) by heating it in a sealed retort. FeSO4.7H2O is 278.03 g/mol; on strong heating it first sheds its 7 waters, then 2 FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3 (a real, balanced decomposition: 2x151.92 = 303.84 g FeSO4 gives 159.7 g Fe2O3 + 64.07 g SO2 + 80.07 g SO3). Only the SO3 half readily condenses with water into strong acid in a chilled receiver; the SO2 half historically escaped or gave a separate, weaker 'spirit of sulphur'. Per kg of starting crystal, the theoretical SO3-derived H2SO4 is 0.176 kg; taking a generous 70% capture in a period retort (real losses were large - gas escapes past every joint) gives 0.1235 kg acid per kg vitriol, hence 7.7 t of vitriol per tonne of ~95%-strength acid. This process ALSO yields a red iron-oxide residue ('colcothar'), used historically as a pigment and polishing rouge, which this entry does not price - it is outside this file's assigned material list. Fuel is a rough estimate for sustained red heat (500-700 C) driving off seven waters of crystallisation and then decomposing the anhydrous salt across many small batches; it is not derived from a measured kiln efficiency the way lime_kg's is, and is the softest number in this entry.

salt_kg.basis: per tonne of mined and crushed rock salt, ~97% NaCl
salt_kg.yield_basis: EXTRACTED, the first of three sources this file treats separately because they are economically nothing alike. Halite is soft (Mohs 2.5), so breaking it is easier per tonne than hard-rock ore even in a deep mine (Wieliczka, Cardona, Hallstatt were worked for centuries on exactly this softness); labour is set closer to cassiterite_kg's alluvial figure than to copper_ore_kg's hard-rock one, with a small allowance added for the deep vertical haulage real rock-salt mines needed. 97% purity reflects typical dressed halite after picking out visible clay/anhydrite bands, with minor crushing loss. Where a workable seam exists, this is the cheapest of the three routes because neither climate nor fuel enters into it at all - only digging.

capital.good: pan levees, puddled-clay lining and sluices
capital.capital_basis: Added deliberately as the CHEAP case, in contrast with the furnaces above: salt_solar_kg's own yield_basis says the process is climate- and land-limited, needing no furnace and essentially no fuel, but a working saltern is still not free of capital - earthen levees dividing the pans, a puddled-clay lining to stop the brine draining into the ground before it concentrates, and timber sluice gates to move water between pans as it concentrates are all real, physical works, just modest ones next to a blast furnace. Ten years is the physical fact that earthen embankments and clay linings erode under wave and weather action and need periodic renewal, not a financial convention; it is markedly longer than any furnace lining above precisely because nothing here is exposed to thermal cycling or chemical attack, only weather. Annual output is representative of a working saltern of a few hectares.

salt_solar_kg.extracted_from: coastal saltern (seawater concentrated by sun and wind)
salt_solar_kg.basis: per tonne of salt raked from solar evaporation pans
salt_solar_kg.yield_basis: EXTRACTED, and CLIMATE- AND LAND-LIMITED rather than fuel-limited - the opposite constraint from salt_brine_kg below. Seawater averages ~3.5% dissolved salt by mass; solar pans do the entire concentration and crystallisation with sun and wind as the only energy input, so no fuel and essentially no chemistry appears in this entry at all. What actually limits a saltern is evaporation rate and pond area, which is a geography fact (insolation, wind, humidity, coastline available) rather than a production recipe - exactly why Mediterranean coasts exported salt and northern European ones taxed it instead. That land/climate scarcity belongs in the rent this file's extracted_from mechanism already provides, the same way an ore deposit's grade sets its rent, rather than in an invented hectare-yield number this entry has no good way to defend. Labour is raking crystallised salt off the pan floor and maintaining the levees and sluices - genuinely light work, since the sun does the work a furnace would otherwise need fuel for.

salt_brine_kg.basis: per tonne of salt boiled dry from a rich brine-spring source
salt_brine_kg.yield_basis: EXTRACTED, and FUEL-LIMITED rather than climate-limited - the reason inland brine-spring salt (Lorraine, Cheshire, Halle, Salins-les-Bains, and Sichuan's brine wells) was consistently the most expensive of the three sources and consumed forests at an industrial scale. Taking a representatively rich spring brine at ~25% NaCl by mass (many productive springs, formed by groundwater dissolving through a buried halite bed, run close to saturation - weaker springs exist too and cost proportionately more fuel), one tonne of dry salt needs 4 t of brine, of which 3 t is water that must be boiled off. Water's latent heat of vaporisation is ~2.26 MJ/kg, so the reaction-free physical minimum is ~6800 MJ; an open pan over a wood fire, uninsulated and continuously topped up, is nowhere near thermally efficient - taking a rough 30% (open pans lose most of their heat to the surrounding air and lose more still through the metal pan itself) scales that to ~22,600 MJ, and at firewood's ~15 MJ/kg calorific value that is about 1500 kg of wood per tonne of salt. This is the single number that explains why brine-boiling towns fought over forest rights the way rock-salt towns never had to. Labour is pan-tending across the long boil; fuel-gathering labour belongs to firewood_kg's own entry, not this one.

alum_kg.basis: per tonne of crystallised potash alum, KAl(SO4)2.12H2O, roasted and leached from alunite ('alum stone')
alum_kg.yield_basis: The historically dominant route (Tolfa in the Papal States, a real medieval/renaissance monopoly industry) roasts alunite ore, KAl3(SO4)2(OH)6 (414.23 g/mol), then leaches it with hot water and crystallises alum on cooling. The elegance of alunite as an alum ore is that it already carries potassium and sulphate in exactly the 1:2 ratio alum needs - KAl(SO4)2.12H2O is 474.46 g/mol, so one mole of alunite gives one mole of alum (a mass GAIN, from twelve waters of crystallisation picked up in the leach liquor), using only one of alunite's three aluminium atoms; the other two-thirds of the aluminium stays behind as an insoluble clay-like residue, which is why alum works always left large waste heaps. Natural alunite deposits run perhaps 40% alunite by mass in gangue rock, and roasting-plus-leaching recovers on the order of 85% of the mineral's alum-forming capacity (incomplete decomposition, leaching loss). Ore tonnage itself is not listed here as a separate material input because this file does not track an 'alunite ore' key of its own and the roast is a single combined pit-to-crystal operation, exactly the way sulfur_kg folds mining and kilning together; the labour figure below is scaled to reflect handling roughly 2.6 t of ore per tonne of alum. Charcoal fires the ~500 C roast that dehydrates and cracks the alunite structure open enough to leach; water is the leach-and-crystallisation liquor, most of which is later reused rather than consumed, but this entry books a generous single-pass figure rather than assuming a recycling loop it cannot verify.

ethanol_kg.basis: per tonne of pure (100% ABV-equivalent) ethanol recovered by malting, fermentation and pot-still distillation of grain
ethanol_kg.yield_basis: Two stoichiometric steps in series. Malt enzymes hydrolyse starch to glucose, (C6H10O5)n + H2O -> C6H12O6 per repeat unit, a 1.11 kg glucose per kg starch theoretical yield taken at 90% real conversion; Gay-Lussac fermentation then runs C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2 CO2 (180.16 g/mol glucose to 92.14 g/mol ethanol, 51.1% theoretical mass yield), taken at 90% of theoretical for yeast losses and unfermented residue - together about 0.46 kg ethanol per kg fermentable sugar. Wheat carries roughly 65% starch by mass, so raw grain gives on the order of 0.30 kg ethanol per kg grain in the fermented wash, close to the ~0.30-0.35 kg/kg long cited for grain whisky distilling. A single pot still does not capture the wash's alcohol quantitatively - heads, tails and an imperfect cut cost on the order of 15% - taking 85% recovery gives the ~0.255 kg/kg net figure behind the 3920 kg grain figure. Mashing water is a standard ~3:1 water:grain ratio, most of which leaves as spent wash rather than appearing in the output. Firewood is a rough estimate for the extended boiling a pot still needs to concentrate and redistill the wash to drinkable/usable proof; it is the softest number in this entry.

dye_kg.extracted_from: arable land (madder root, Rubia tinctorum, a 2-3 year crop)
dye_kg.basis: per tonne of dried, ground natural dyestuff, standing in for the tree's single generic 'dye_kg' key
dye_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (rule 3.4): real historical dyestuffs varied enormously in cost - madder red, woad and indigo blue, kermes and cochineal crimson, murex purple are not remotely the same economics, and this one key cannot represent all of them honestly. Madder root is taken as the representative case because it was the single most widely grown and traded natural dye in pre-modern agriculture. Madder is a 2-3 year root crop; historical cultivation (Alsace, the Netherlands) is commonly cited at 1500-2500 kg of dried root per hectare over the growing cycle, taken here at 2000 kg over 2.5 years, i.e. 800 kg dried root per hectare per year. Grinding and screening out the woody core loses roughly 10% of that mass, giving 720 kg/ha/yr of usable ground dyestuff, which this entry states as its per-tonne basis scaled up (720 kg/ha/yr means 1.39 ha-years of cultivation per tonne of output). Labour is dominated by root-lifting, which is notoriously heavy work because madder roots grow up to 2 m deep - not as extreme as cotton_kg's hand-picking, but a genuinely labour-hungry crop next to a cereal.

water_kg.extracted_from: river, spring or well (fresh water at the point of use)
water_kg.basis: per tonne of fresh water hauled from a nearby source
water_kg.yield_basis: This is a GEOGRAPHY fact, not a production recipe, and is deliberately not treated as one - there is no chemistry or physical transformation in drawing water. The labour figure here (half an hour to haul a tonne by hand from a river bank or a shallow well) is only the baseline case of a settlement sited on water. What actually sets water's real cost - a desert caravan town paying camel-loads of water a very long way, versus a riverside town where it is nearly free - is DISTANCE AND LIFT from the source, which is a transport/rent fact belonging to wherever this simulator prices geography and haulage, not something this entry should fake by inventing a recipe. Treat this entry as the cheap end of a range whose expensive end this file does not attempt to compute.

bleach_kg.basis: per tonne of bleaching powder ('chloride of lime'), calcium hypochlorite/chloride absorbed onto slaked lime
bleach_kg.yield_basis: Two reactions in series, both balanced. Scheele's 1774 method generates chlorine from pyrolusite and hydrochloric acid: MnO2 (86.94 g/mol) + 4 HCl (145.84 g/mol pure) -> MnCl2 + Cl2 (70.90 g/mol) + 2 H2O; per kg Cl2 that is 1.226 kg pure MnO2 (1.53 kg at pyrolusite_kg's own 80% assay) and 2.06 kg pure HCl (6.86 kg at hydrochloric_acid_kg's ~30% commercial strength), scaled here by an 85% generator efficiency for incomplete reaction and gas loss. The gas is then absorbed onto slaked lime, Cl2 + Ca(OH)2 -> CaOCl2 + H2O (a 1.79 kg bleaching-powder yield per kg Cl2, needing 1.045 kg Ca(OH)2, i.e. 0.79 kg of lime_kg's quicklime once slaking water is subtracted out), taken at 90% absorption efficiency in the lime bed. As a cross-check: pure CaOCl2 is 55.8% chlorine by mass, and the conventional industrial assay of 'available chlorine' (roughly half of total combined chlorine, the historically standard commercial spec) comes out near 30%, which matches the widely cited 35%-available-chlorine grade of real 19th-century bleaching powder reasonably well. This entry deliberately consumes hydrochloric_acid_kg rather than describing chlorine as if it fell from the sky - it is a genuinely expensive input, which is exactly why the later Deacon and electrolytic chlorine processes existed to escape Scheele's HCl consumption.

hydrogen_m3.basis: per 1000 normal cubic metres (0 C, 1 atm) of hydrogen gas generated by iron and dilute sulphuric acid
hydrogen_m3.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRIC, and the historically attested early route - iron filings and dilute sulphuric acid, the method behind the first hydrogen balloon (Charles, 1783). Fe + H2SO4 -> FeSO4 + H2; one mole of H2 (22.414 L at STP) needs 55.85 g iron and 98.08 g pure H2SO4. Scaling 1000 Nm3 (44,615 mol) gives 2492 kg iron and 4376 kg pure acid, i.e. 6732 kg of this file's 65%-strength chamber acid; a 90% capture allowance for gas lost during collection over water gives the figures above. No separate fuel is needed - the reaction is mildly exothermic and runs at room temperature - so energy_mj is zero and labour is only charging the generator and tending the gas holder. Mass conservation is not checkable here because the output is a gas volume, not a weight.

hydrochloric_acid_kg.basis: per tonne of hydrochloric acid at ~30% HCl by mass (commercial 'muriatic acid' strength), from the Leblanc 'salt cake' reaction
hydrochloric_acid_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRIC: 2 NaCl + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2 HCl (2x58.44 + 98.08 = 215.0 g reactants against 142.04 + 2x36.46 = 215.0 g products - balanced). Per kg of pure HCl this needs 1.60 kg salt and 1.35 kg pure H2SO4 (2.07 kg of this file's 65%-strength chamber acid); at 30% output strength a tonne contains 300 kg pure HCl, giving 481 kg salt and 621 kg acid before losses. Real muffle-furnace HCl generation vents a substantial fraction of the gas rather than capturing it - this was a genuine, well-documented 19th-century problem (untreated Leblanc-works HCl fumes were toxic enough that Britain's Alkali Act 1863 was passed specifically to force its capture), and taking 85% capture (representing works fitted with Gossage absorption towers rather than earlier plants that simply vented it) scales the figures to those given. The same reaction also deposits solid sodium sulphate ('salt cake') in the furnace, which historically fed the Leblanc soda industry (see sodium_carbonate_kg) - not credited here as a joint output, since this entry is written to price HCl on its own account rather than as a soda-works by-product. Coal fires the muffle furnace, which must reach red heat to drive the second, harder stage of the reaction (NaCl + NaHSO4 -> Na2SO4 + HCl) to completion.

ammonia_kg.basis: per tonne of ammonia liberated from coke-oven 'gas liquor'
ammonia_kg.yield_basis: Pre-Haber-Bosch ammonia was overwhelmingly a BY-PRODUCT of coking coal for coke and town gas, not something made on its own account - bituminous coal carries roughly 1-1.5% nitrogen by mass, most of which stays in the coke or tar, and only a small fraction is driven off and captured as ammonia. The widely cited historical benchmark is on the order of 2.5-3.5 kg of ammonium sulphate ((NH4)2SO4, 25.8% NH3 by mass) recovered per tonne of coal carbonised in a byproduct coke oven, i.e. roughly 0.75-1 kg of NH3 per tonne of coal - taken here as 0.75 kg/t, which is why the coal figure above is so large. Lime is added to the collected ammonia liquor to liberate free ammonia gas from the fixed ammonium salts it is dissolved as (2 NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCl2 + 2 NH3 + 2 H2O and its sulphate analogue), at a stoichiometric ~1.65 kg of quicklime per kg of NH3 released. LABELLED HEURISTIC (rule 3.4): this entry charges the full cost of the coal input, which is not how a byproduct is really priced - the coking itself would be happening anyway to make coke and gas, and a properly joint-costed entry would split the coal's cost across coke, gas, tar and ammonia the way lead_kg/silver_kg split galena's cost across lead and silver. Doing that correctly means giving coal_kg's own entry (in a different file this task does not touch) multiple outputs, which this entry cannot do. This is by a wide margin the least confident entry in this file.

oxygen_m3.extracted_from: atmosphere (cryogenic fractional distillation of liquid air, the Linde process)
oxygen_m3.basis: per 1000 normal cubic metres (0 C, 1 atm) of gaseous oxygen separated from air
oxygen_m3.yield_basis: Air liquefies under compression and Joule-Thomson expansion, and oxygen (boiling point -183 C) and nitrogen (-196 C) then separate by fractional distillation of the liquid - a physics fact, not a recipe, hence no material inputs and extracted_from naming the atmosphere itself as the free source, the same way water_kg and iugerum_land treat their sources. The theoretical minimum separation work (the Gibbs free energy of unmixing air) is small, well under 1 MJ/m3, but real early Linde-process plants (from 1902) ran far above that minimum because compressors and heat exchangers of the period were nowhere near ideal - roughly 2 kWh (7.2 MJ) per normal cubic metre of oxygen is a representative figure for that generation of equipment, a full order of magnitude above the thermodynamic floor and several times a modern cryogenic air-separation unit's figure. This is a plant-efficiency estimate rather than a physical constant, and is the softest number in the entry. Mass conservation is not checkable here because the output is a gas volume, not a weight. Carried as mechanical_mj, not thermal_mj: a Linde-process compressor is a piece of rotating machinery doing shaft work (historically belt- or motor-driven), not a firebox - see ENERGY in sim/solve_prices.py's module docstring.

blue_vitriol_kg.basis: per tonne of crystallised copper sulphate pentahydrate (CuSO4.5H2O)
blue_vitriol_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRIC. Hot, concentrated sulphuric acid is itself the oxidant that lets copper metal (which does not react with dilute acid) dissolve: Cu + 2 H2SO4(conc.,hot) -> CuSO4 + SO2 + 2 H2O (63.55 + 196.16 = 259.71 g reactants against 159.61 + 64.07 + 36.03 = 259.71 g products - balanced), and the sulphate then crystallises with five waters, CuSO4 + 5 H2O -> CuSO4.5H2O (249.69 g/mol). Per kg of crystal that is 0.2545 kg copper and 0.7857 kg pure H2SO4 (1.209 kg at 65% chamber strength); a 90% allowance for unreacted copper and crystallisation loss gives the figures above. Charcoal is a rough estimate for the heat needed to keep the acid hot and concentrated enough to act as an oxidiser (concentrated H2SO4 only oxidises copper well above room temperature), not a derived kiln-efficiency figure.

paint_kg.basis: per tonne of oil paint, ground pigment suspended in a drying oil
paint_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (rule 3.4). Historical oil paint is pigment ground into a drying oil at roughly equal parts by mass (formulations ranged 40-60% pigment depending on pigment density and desired consistency; 50/50 is taken as the representative mid-point), a simple mechanical mulling with essentially no mass loss. This dataset has no linseed_oil_kg or other true drying-oil material - only olive_oil_kg, which chemically is NOT a drying oil (it is dominated by oleic acid and will not oxidise/polymerise into a paint film the way linseed's linolenic-acid-rich composition does) - so olive_oil_kg stands in as the only tracked vegetable oil, a real simplification rather than a claim that ancient painters actually used olive oil this way. mineral_pigment_kg is this file's own entry for ground natural earth pigment. Labour is grinding pigment into the oil with a muller by hand, plus a skilled colour-mixer's judgement of consistency.

formaldehyde_kg.basis: per tonne of formaldehyde gas/solution from catalytic oxidation of wood-distillation methanol
formaldehyde_kg.yield_basis: Two stages, both real 19th-century technology. Destructive (retort) distillation of dry hardwood yields 'wood alcohol' (methanol) at roughly 1.0-1.5% of the wood's dry mass, taken here at 1.2%, alongside the same charcoal and tar a traditional clamp burn also produces. Methanol is then partially oxidised over a hot silver or copper catalyst (Loew/Tollens process, from 1889), CH3OH + 1/2 O2 -> HCHO + H2O (32.04 -> 30.03 g/mol, 93.7% theoretical mass yield), taken at 85% of theoretical for real catalytic conversion. Combined, that is roughly 9.6 kg of formaldehyde per tonne of dry wood processed, hence the large wood figure. LABELLED HEURISTIC (rule 3.4): this entry charges the full wood input to formaldehyde alone and does not credit the charcoal, tar and acetic acid the same retort run also yields - a fully joint-costed version would follow lead_kg/silver_kg's pattern and share the wood's cost across all four streams, which this entry does not attempt. Charcoal fuels the catalytic converter itself, a small addition next to the wood tonnage.

acetic_acid_kg.basis: per tonne of glacial acetic acid recovered via the 'acetate of lime' process
acetic_acid_kg.yield_basis: The major 19th-century industrial route before synthetic acetic acid: the same destructive distillation of wood that gives methanol and charcoal (see formaldehyde_kg) also yields pyroligneous liquor containing acetic acid, commonly cited at 6-10% of dry wood mass in the crude liquor; after purification losses a net recovery on the order of 5% of dry wood mass as usable acid is taken here, giving the 20 t wood figure. The crude acid is neutralised with lime to precipitate calcium acetate (2 CH3COOH + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(C2H3O2)2 + 2 H2O), which is then decomposed with sulphuric acid to liberate concentrated acid and gypsum (Ca(C2H3O2)2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2 CH3COOH) - stoichiometrically 0.617 kg Ca(OH)2 (0.467 kg as lime_kg's quicklime) and 0.817 kg pure H2SO4 (1.256 kg at 65% strength) per kg of acid recovered. LABELLED HEURISTIC (rule 3.4): as with formaldehyde_kg, this entry charges the full wood cost without crediting the charcoal co-product from the same retort run. Charcoal fuel here is for the acid-liberation redistillation, not the primary wood pyrolysis, which is self-firing.

calcium_carbide_kg.basis: per tonne of calcium carbide (CaC2) from the electric-arc furnace (Willson process, 1892)
calcium_carbide_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRIC: CaO + 3 C -> CaC2 + CO (56.08 + 36.03 = 92.11 g reactants against 64.10 + 28.01 = 92.11 g products - balanced). Per kg of carbide that is 0.875 kg quicklime and 0.562 kg carbon; taking an 85% arc-furnace conversion efficiency gives the figures above (charcoal stands in for the metallurgical coke a real plant would use, since coke is not itself a tracked material here - a minor simplification). The defining fact about this process is that it is almost entirely an ELECTRICITY consumer rather than a fuel-heat one: the arc furnace must reach roughly 2000 C, well above anything a combustion furnace reaches, and historically consumed on the order of 3000-4000 kWh per tonne of carbide - a benchmark still roughly true of modern carbide furnaces - taken here at 3500 kWh (12,600 MJ). This entry is only reachable once cheap, abundant electricity exists, which is itself the real historical constraint on carbide (and hence acetylene) availability - carried as electrical_mj so that constraint is exactly what sim/solve_prices.py's electrical energy market now prices. ELECTRICAL, NOT SHAFT WORK: this figure is carried as electrical_mj because the process is electrolysis or an electric furnace, which needs an electric current rather than a turning shaft. It was originally written as mechanical_mj on the reasoning that electricity must bottom out in whatever turns the dynamo - true for a waterwheel, false in general, since a photovoltaic panel makes current from photons with no shaft anywhere. See Complaints/39 and the ENERGY section of sim/solve_prices.py.

acetylene_kg.basis: per tonne of acetylene gas from calcium carbide and water
acetylene_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRIC and close to quantitative: CaC2 + 2 H2O -> Ca(OH)2 + C2H2 (64.10 + 36.03 = 100.13 g reactants against 74.10 + 26.04 = 100.14 g products - balanced). Per kg of acetylene that is 2.462 kg carbide and 1.384 kg water; a 95% allowance covers minor generator losses in an otherwise simple, well-behaved gas-generator reaction (the carbide-lamp reaction, familiar from miners' lamps and early bicycle/car lights). The calcium hydroxide by-product ('carbide sludge') is a low-value waste this entry does not price further.

boric_acid_kg.extracted_from: fumarole steam / natural hot springs (Larderello-type boric-acid lagoons)
boric_acid_kg.basis: per tonne of boric acid crystallised from volcanic-steam lagoon water
boric_acid_kg.yield_basis: EXTRACTED, and a genuinely unusual source worth stating plainly: before borax-lake deposits (Death Valley, from the 1880s) became the dominant source, boric acid came almost entirely from the Larderello district in Tuscany, where volcanic steam ('soffioni') naturally carries boron compounds that dissolve into shallow lagoon water; the water is then evaporated to crystallise the acid. Nature supplies both the boron and, once fumarole steam itself is piped in as the heat source (as the works did once nearby forests were exhausted - a real historical fuel transition worth noting even though it is not separately priced here), most of the evaporation energy too, which is why this is extracted_from rather than a fuelled recipe. Labour is tending the lagoons and scraping/drying the crystallised acid over an extended natural evaporation cycle.

citric_acid_kg.basis: per tonne of citric acid recovered from lemon juice by the lime-precipitation process
citric_acid_kg.yield_basis: New intermediate this file needs for sodium_citrate_kg. The pre-fermentation (pre-1919) industrial route: lemon juice, typically 5-8% citric acid by mass (taken at 6%), is treated with lime to precipitate insoluble calcium citrate (2 C6H8O7 + 3 Ca(OH)2 -> Ca3(C6H5O7)2 + 6 H2O), which is then decomposed with sulphuric acid to release free citric acid and gypsum (Ca3(C6H5O7)2 + 3 H2SO4 -> 2 C6H8O7 + 3 CaSO4) - stoichiometrically 0.579 kg Ca(OH)2 (0.438 kg as lime_kg) and 0.766 kg pure H2SO4 (1.178 kg at 65% strength) per kg of acid recovered, at close to full stoichiometric efficiency since this is straightforward aqueous chemistry. LABELLED HEURISTIC (rule 3.4): growing and juicing the lemons is folded into this entry's labour figure rather than priced as its own land-limited crop the way olive_oil_kg is - a real simplification, accepted here because this material serves only one low-priority downstream node (sodium_citrate_kg).

sodium_carbonate_kg.basis: per tonne of soda ash (Na2CO3) by the Leblanc process
sodium_carbonate_kg.yield_basis: New intermediate (rule 3.4, and see this file's note on why it exists). STOICHIOMETRIC, in two stages, exactly as the task brief asks to show. Stage 1, the salt-cake reaction: 2 NaCl + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2 HCl. Stage 2, the 'black ash' furnace reaction: Na2SO4 + 2 C + CaCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CaS + 2 CO2 (142.04 + 24.02 + 100.09 = 266.15 g reactants against 105.99 + 72.14 + 88.02 = 266.15 g products - balanced). Chaining both stages per kg of soda ash gives 1.103 kg salt, 0.925 kg pure H2SO4 (1.424 kg at 65% strength), 0.227 kg carbon (0.252 kg charcoal) and 0.944 kg limestone; a 75% overall process efficiency (the Leblanc black-ash furnace was notoriously incomplete and labour-brutal, one reason Solvay displaced it within a generation) scales these to the figures above. Extra coal fires the reverberatory furnace itself, beyond the stoichiometric carbon reductant. Stage 1's hydrochloric acid is a genuine co-product of this reaction (see hydrochloric_acid_kg's own note) not credited here, and stage 2's calcium sulphide waste ('galligu') was a real and notorious pollutant of Leblanc works, disposed of rather than priced.

sodium_carbonate_solvay_kg.basis: per tonne of soda ash (Na2CO3) by the Solvay ammonia-soda process
sodium_carbonate_solvay_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRIC. The per-pass reactions are NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O -> NaHCO3 + NH4Cl and 2 NaHCO3 -> Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2, but ammonia is recovered from the NH4Cl by-product with lime (NH4Cl + Ca(OH)2 -> CaCl2 + NH3 + H2O) and recycled, so the textbook NET reaction across the whole plant is 2 NaCl + CaCO3 -> Na2CO3 + CaCl2 (116.88 + 100.09 = 216.97 g reactants against 105.99 + 110.98 = 216.97 g products - balanced), needing 1.103 kg salt and 0.944 kg limestone per kg of soda ash at 100% utilisation. Real single-pass salt utilisation runs on the order of 70-75% (some salt-bearing brine is purged to the famous, environmentally notorious CaCl2 waste ponds rather than fully converted - taken at 72%), which is why the salt figure above exceeds stoichiometric while limestone, whose calcium ends up as either product CO2 or waste CaCl2 either way, is left near-stoichiometric. Ammonia is catalytic in principle but real plants lose a few percent per pass to leaks and purge streams - taken at 2% of the stoichiometric NH3 requirement, linking to this file's own ammonia_kg entry. Limestone is calcined in a lime kiln exactly as lime_kg's own entry describes, both for its CO2 (fed to the carbonating tower) and its CaO (used to recover ammonia), so the coal figure reuses lime_kg's own coal:limestone ratio (450:1800). Labour is markedly lower than the Leblanc entry's - the Solvay process's continuous, far less manual operation is a real, well-documented reason it displaced Leblanc commercially within a generation. The small thermal_mj figure is the residual process heat for the carbonating tower and the ammonia-recovery still beyond what the coal input (already sized to the lime kiln's own ratio) accounts for - ordinary combustion heat, not shaft work, hence thermal rather than mechanical; see ENERGY in sim/solve_prices.py's module docstring.

sodium_citrate_kg.basis: per tonne of trisodium citrate from neutralising citric acid with soda ash
sodium_citrate_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRIC: 2 C6H8O7 + 3 Na2CO3 -> 2 Na3C6H5O7 + 3 H2O + 3 CO2 (384.24 + 317.97 = 702.21 g reactants against 516.14 + 54.05 + 132.03 = 702.22 g products - balanced), 0.744 kg citric acid and 0.616 kg soda ash per kg of product; a 92% allowance for a straightforward aqueous neutralisation and crystallisation gives the figures above. Both inputs are this file's own entries (citric_acid_kg, sodium_carbonate_kg), so this entry is a short final step on top of two already-argued chains rather than a fresh derivation of its own.

chrome_salts_kg.basis: per tonne of sodium dichromate (Na2Cr2O7), the tanning/dyeing/mordanting chemical this generic key most plausibly represents
chrome_salts_kg.yield_basis: Two balanced stages: an oxidising roast of chromite ore with soda ash and air, 4 FeCr2O4 + 8 Na2CO3 + 7 O2 -> 8 Na2CrO4 + 2 Fe2O3 + 8 CO2 (895.36 g reactants against 1967.3 g - the extra mass is the oxygen absorbed, correctly balanced), followed by acidification of the chromate to dichromate, 2 Na2CrO4 + H2SO4 -> Na2Cr2O7 + Na2SO4 + H2O (422.03 g both sides). Chaining these gives 1.237 kg sodium chromate and hence, via the roast, 0.855 kg of pure FeCr2O4 and 0.809 kg soda ash per kg of dichromate, plus 0.374 kg pure H2SO4 (0.576 kg at 65% strength) for acidification; an 80% overall multi-stage efficiency (chrome chemical manufacture was a genuinely difficult, low-yield, hazardous 19th-century industry) gives the soda-ash and acid figures above. INCOMPLETE BY DESIGN (rule 3.4): this entry does NOT charge for the chromite ore itself (roughly 1.9-2.4 kg of dressed ~45%-grade ore per kg of product) because chromite is not defined as its own tracked material here the way calamine_kg or galena_kg were for other ores in 20_nonferrous.json - a properly complete entry would add that. Charcoal is a rough estimate for the prolonged, high-temperature oxidising roast, which historically was very fuel-hungry; it is not derived from a measured efficiency. This is, along with ammonia_kg, the least confident entry in this file.

mineral_pigment_kg.extracted_from: quarry / clay pit (iron-oxide-bearing earth - ochre, umber, sienna)
mineral_pigment_kg.basis: per tonne of washed, ground natural earth pigment
mineral_pigment_kg.yield_basis: EXTRACTED. Natural iron-oxide earth pigments need no chemistry to use as-is - digging, washing (levigation, to float off sand and grit) and grinding to a fine powder is the whole process for yellow/brown ochres. Where a red pigment is wanted, a light roast dehydrates goethite to hematite (2 FeO(OH) -> Fe2O3 + H2O, a simple, well-known colour-change roast) but this adds only a modest fuel cost this entry does not itemise separately, folded into the labour figure as a rough allowance. Labour is digging, washing and grinding - comparable to limestone_kg's and clay_kg's own figures for quarried earth materials.

resin_kg.basis: per tonne of raw pine resin (oleoresin) collected by tapping standing trees
resin_kg.yield_basis: New intermediate this file needs for varnish_kg. EXTRACTED - resin tapping ('turpentining') cuts a wound in the bark and lets the tree's own resin bleed slowly into a collecting cup over a season, with no chemistry and no fuel involved. Yield per tree is small and collection is unavoidably slow and seasonal, which is reflected in the labour figure - a real, well-documented feature of the historical naval-stores (pine resin, tar, pitch, turpentine) trade rather than a furnace or recipe constraint.

varnish_kg.basis: per tonne of cooked oil-resin varnish
varnish_kg.yield_basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC (rule 3.4) on the oil component only. Historical varnish is pine or other tree resin melted and cooked together with a hot drying oil until fused - roughly equal parts by mass is representative of period oil varnishes, taken here as 45% resin (this file's own resin_kg) to 55% oil. olive_oil_kg again stands in for a true drying oil, as in paint_kg, with the same caveat that olive oil is not chemically a drying oil (it lacks linseed's linolenic-acid-driven oxidative polymerisation) - the only vegetable oil this dataset tracks. Labour is dominated by the genuinely dangerous, fire-prone business of cooking hot oil and resin together over a controlled flame, a real hazard of the historical varnish trade; charcoal fuels that cook.

asbestos_kg.basis: per tonne of milled, air-classified asbestos fibre
asbestos_kg.yield_basis: EXTRACTED, and purely mechanical - no chemistry is involved anywhere in this entry, unlike almost everything else in this file. Chrysotile forms as fibrous veins within serpentine rock; after mining, the rock is crushed and the light fibre is separated from the much heavier waste rock by mechanical milling and air classification (fibre floats in an air stream, rock dust does not). Labour splits between hard-rock mining of the vein and the milling/classifying stage, comparable in kind to calamine_kg's and galena_kg's dressing labour for other ores.

celluloid_kg.basis: per tonne of celluloid (plasticised cellulose nitrate) sheet
celluloid_kg.yield_basis: A 70:30 nitrocellulose-to-camphor ratio by mass is the historically attested Hyatt formulation (1869-70): camphor physically plasticises nitrocellulose by disrupting inter-chain hydrogen bonding, which is what gives celluloid its characteristic thermoplastic mouldability rather than nitrocellulose's own brittleness. This is purely a physical blend under heat and pressure, not a chemical reaction, so the ratio - not stoichiometry - is the physical fact here, and mass is conserved almost exactly aside from a small solvent loss. Alcohol is used during manufacture to gelatinise the mixture before hot-rolling and is mostly recovered and reused, so only a small net consumption is booked. nitrocellulose_kg HAS NO PRODUCTION ENTRY IN THIS FILE - out of scope by instruction, a deliberate, recorded gap, the same treatment this file gives nitric_acid_kg elsewhere. This entry only says how much of it celluloid needs, never how to make it.

camphor_kg.basis: per tonne of camphor recovered by steam-distilling chipped camphor-laurel (Cinnamomum camphora) wood
camphor_kg.yield_basis: New intermediate this file needs for celluloid_kg. Camphor-laurel heartwood carries roughly 2-4% camphor by mass (older trees richer), taken at a middling 2.5%, with steam distillation recovering on the order of 85% of that content - a net 2.125% yield, meaning roughly 47 t of chipped heartwood processed per tonne of camphor recovered, hence the large wood figure (wood_kg is this file's existing raw-feedstock material, already used the same way by charcoal_kg). Labour is dominated by chipping that much wood and tending prolonged steam-still batches; charcoal raises the steam.

phosphorus_red_kg.basis: per tonne of red phosphorus, converted from white phosphorus reduced from bone ash in an electric or fuel-fired retort
phosphorus_red_kg.yield_basis: STOICHIOMETRIC retort reduction, the historical (Scheele/Gahn-derived, industrialised mid-1800s) route before electric-furnace phosphorus: 2 Ca3(PO4)2 + 6 SiO2 + 10 C -> 6 CaSiO3 + 10 CO + P4 (1100.94 g reactants against 1100.96 g products - balanced). Per kg of white phosphorus that is 5.01 kg pure Ca3(PO4)2 (6.26 kg at bone ash's ~80% assay), 2.91 kg silica (sand_quartz_kg, taken near-pure) and 0.97 kg carbon (1.08 kg as charcoal); a 65% real retort yield (this reduction runs at 1400-1500 C and any leak lets phosphorus vapour escape and oxidise before condensing, historically a genuinely difficult and dangerous process) scales these up. White phosphorus is then converted to the red allotrope by prolonged heating at 250-300 C in the absence of air - no reagent is consumed, only heat, but a further 5% is lost to sublimation and venting during the slow conversion. Extra charcoal beyond the stoichiometric reductant fires the retort itself, which must sustain a far higher temperature than any other roast in this file. Phosphorus manufacture was a severe historical occupational hazard (industrial phosphorus poisoning, 'phossy jaw', among 19th-century match-workers), reflected here in the heavy furnaceman labour figure rather than in any material line.

argon_or_h2_m3.basis: per 1000 normal cubic metres of inert/reducing furnace or lamp-fill gas, priced via the cheaper of the two named alternatives
argon_or_h2_m3.yield_basis: DATA-CATEGORISATION FLAG, worth raising rather than quietly working around: this key conflates two chemically unrelated gases (argon and hydrogen) that can serve the same functional role - an inert or reducing atmosphere for a furnace, lamp or bulb - under one material. Argon (0.93% of air by volume) is only recoverable as a side-fraction of the same cryogenic air-separation plant that this file's oxygen_m3 entry describes, a technology that postdates argon's own 1894 discovery (Rayleigh and Ramsay) and was historically both later-arriving and more expensive than the alternative. Hydrogen, by contrast, is available far earlier and more cheaply by the same iron-and-acid reaction as this file's own hydrogen_m3 entry. Since a generic material key should be priced at its cheapest available source rather than an arbitrary one, this entry simply reuses hydrogen_m3's identical stoichiometry and figures rather than re-deriving them. Recommend to the project that this key be split into its two real materials once anything needs to distinguish them - an application that specifically needs an inert (non-flammable) atmosphere cannot actually substitute hydrogen for argon, and this entry cannot express that constraint.
